full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** A recent preprint describes this system and every headline number you list. The one caveat is that it is a single-author arXiv preprint, not yet peer-reviewed as far as I can tell.

**1. Model family.** This is pulse-coupled integrate-and-fire oscillators with all-to-all coupling, in the Peskin / Mirollo–Strogatz tradition. The charging curve is linear, with no leak. Pulse size is k/N for a firing cluster of size k. Oscillators pushed to threshold are absorbed into the firing cluster. Your system is the linear-charging boundary case between synchronizing and clustering regimes.

**2. The specific behaviour.** O'Keeffe's preprint (arXiv:2609.01668, "Arithmetic of the sync basin for pulse-coupled oscillators", submitted 1 Sep 2026, v2 30 Sep 2026) describes all of the following.
- The synchronization probability is P_sync = A_{N,1}/N^N for all N, where A_{N,1} satisfies an exact recurrence.
- For prime N, P_sync = 1 − 1/N^N. For composite N, 1 − P_sync ~ C_m N^{-(m−1)}, where m is the smallest prime divisor.
- Check against your numbers: N=5 gives 1 − 1/3125 = 0.99968, which matches. For even N, m = 2, so the exponent is 1, which matches. The paper gives empirical prefactors C₂ ≈ 0.60 and C₃ ≈ 0.53, so your prefactor of 0.6 matches. For N divisible by 3 but not 2, the exponent is 2.
- It also states an "equal-size principle": every non-synchronizing trajectory settles into equal-size clusters whose common size divides N, with K clusters each of size N/K. Every divisor is realized, so the number of distinct outcomes is exactly d(N). Your 9 final states at N=100 equal d(100)=9.
- For primes, the only non-sync outcome is the all-singleton state.
- The paper treats the power-law prefactors and exponent as empirical. It says a proof of the scaling law is still open. Your exponent and prefactor are therefore matched, but not rigorously derived.

**Earlier and related sources.**
- Mirollo & Strogatz 1990, SIAM J. Appl. Math. 50(6):1645–1662, "Synchronization of Pulse-Coupled Biological Oscillators". For almost all initial conditions, the population evolves to all oscillators firing synchronously. This is the foundational model, but it requires a concave-down charging curve, so it does not cover the linear case.
- Díaz-Guilera, Pérez & Arenas, arXiv:cond-mat/9607056, "Synchronization of Integrate and Fire oscillators with global coupling". They study linear and concave integrate-and-fire oscillators with additive global pulse coupling of strength nδ and δ ∝ 1/N. They state that the system synchronizes completely unless the two last remaining groups are of equal sizes. That is an early partial precursor of the equal-size mechanism. I did not confirm the journal venue from the search results.
- Strogatz and O'Keeffe, "Synchronization as Aggregation: Cluster Kinetics of Pulse-Coupled Oscillators", Phys. Rev. E 93, 032203 (2016). The arXiv version (1510.05341) is titled "Transient dynamics of pulse-coupled oscillators with nonlinear charging curves". This is the closest review-like source. It treats identical all-to-all integrate-and-fire oscillators where clusters can only grow and never break apart. It is a kinetic (large-N) treatment, and I did not verify that it contains the divisor or prime result. I identified the journal from the APS accepted-manuscript URL, not from a full citation record.
- Senn & Urbanczik 2001 (SIAM J. Appl. Math. 61:1143–1155), "Similar non-leaky integrate-and-fire neurons with instantaneous couplings always synchronize". It concerns a related non-leaky case with non-identical neurons or different couplings. It is not the same system and does not contradict the equal-cluster result.

**3. Confidence: medium-high.** The preprint matches your rules (k/N kicks, absorption, linear charging), the prime closed form, the exponent 1 and prefactor of about 0.60, and the divisor count. I read these in the search excerpts, not the full paper. I did not find a peer-reviewed venue for it. I also cannot rule out earlier work containing the same arithmetic (divisor structure, prime closed form) that my searches missed. The Díaz-Guilera et al. remark only partly anticipates it.
